To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the hot-dark spot index (HDS), which is a normalized difference between the two directional signatures, can be linearly linked to the vegetation clumping index, which is a key descriptor of vegetation structure, and that this relationship is consistent across three vegetation types (broadleaf, conifer, and grassland).
the hot dark spot index (HDS) can be used to retrieve the clumping index for different vegetation types, which in turn can be used to estimate canopy photosynthesis.

the hot spot and the dark spot signatures measured in the backscattered and forward scattered regions, respectively, of the bidirectional radiance distribution function can be used to retrieve the clumping index of vegetation, which is a key parameter for the estimation of canopy productivity.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: 1) the formulation of a new directional index, HDS, based on the two most important directional reflectance signatures, the hot spot and the dark spot, which can discriminate vegetation types and 2) the validation of the HDS using the BEPS model and the POLDER data set.
the development and evaluation of a new approach to map the vegetation clumping index based on the hot spot signatures observed by the POLDER instrument.
a new approach for retrieving the vegetation clumping index at global scale using hot spot signatures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, for the first time, the POLDER hot spot signatures have been used to retrieve the clumping index at global scale.
the HDS, a directional signature, can be used to retrieve vegetation clumping index, which is an important ecological descriptor of vegetation.
, in spite of the limitations of the data set used, the HDS index is able to discriminate between vegetation types, with the potential to retrieve the clumping index.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the POLDER hot spot and dark spots are useful for the retrieval of vegetation clumping information.
the hot spot signature can be used as a potential indicator of the clumping effect in vegetation, which has not been reported previously.

we have shown that a simple index derived from the hot spot and the dark spot of reflectance measured by the spaceborne polarimeters can be related to the clumping index, which is a key parameter in the canopy photosynthesis modeling and in turn the terrestrial productivity assessment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
hot spot signatures can be used to retrieve vegetation clumping information at a global scale, which is a key parameter to improve the estimation of terrestrial productivity.
the HDS is a robust index that can be retrieved from space and that can be used to map the foliage clumping in vegetation canopies.
the POLDER hot spot signatures can be exploited to map the clumping index at global scale, which is a critical input to improve the accuracy of ecosystem models.
